records.name: The chemical marks on one gene are rewritten in a person, with no cut in the DNA

missing.what: A second company, Epicrispr Biotechnologies, has a trial in people of a treatment of this kind, aimed at one of a person's own genes in a muscle-wasting disease. Its release of 2026-06-26 says nine people had been treated, that the first three to reach six months had gained muscle on scans, and that a blood marker tied to the target gene had fallen (no figures). The registry entry (NCT06907875) shows a start of 2025-05-08, 12 people, active and no longer recruiting, last updated 2026-08-19, no results posted. Neither the entry nor anything in data/ mentions this company or trial.
missing.why: It bears on the first-human test but does not meet it: the test asks for 'a peer-reviewed report or a trial registry's posted results', and this is a company release (read as the copy on a patient society's site, because the wire service refused the fetch). It is a second trial that could reach the rung, so the first-human years rest on more than one programme.

missing.what: A trade article dated 2026-10-05 says the same company presented six-month findings from six people at a congress in Japan, with twelve-month findings promised for the second half of 2027. Seen in a search summary only.

The entry does not mention it; the weekly reading of 2026-10-18 names the company only for an animal study.
missing.why: A dose alone does not meet the test, which asks for a measured change lasting six months in a peer-reviewed report or posted results. Three companies now have people dosed where the estimate reasons from one, which makes an early peer-reviewed human report somewhat more likely.

missing.what: The registry entry for the trial the entry names (NCT06671093) gives an estimated primary completion of 2028-06-28 and study completion of 2028-10-30, with 36 people estimated. The entry's notes do not give these dates.

records.name: A mix of small-molecule drugs resets a cell's age without gene therapy

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in the journal Aging (Kato and colleagues, 2025-08-21) gave frail 25-month-old mice a mix of two small molecules, with no genes delivered: an inhibitor of a signalling pathway that rises with age, together with the hormone oxytocin. From the start of treatment the treated male mice lived 73 per cent longer, their median lifespan across the whole study was 14 per cent greater, and they did better on physical performance, endurance, short-term memory and resistance to death; the benefit appeared in males and not females. The entry does not mention it, and the only mentions of oxytocin anywhere in data/ are passing ones in two other treatments' notes.
missing.why: On a plain reading it could meet the animal rung: 'a living animal given a mix of small-molecule drugs, with no genes delivered', with 'a restored tissue function' moved towards youth against untreated controls, in a peer-reviewed report. What is unclear is whether the entry means its mix to be a cell-resetting one; this mix was given to correct two age-related signals, not to reset cell age, and the paper reports no clock of cell age. If it counts, the animal rung was reached in 2025, four years before the likely year of 2029.

missing.what: Another peer-reviewed report in Aging and Disease (Schwarz and colleagues, 2026-10-09), from a randomised placebo-controlled trial, gave a single substance (spermidine) rather than a mix, so it does not bear on this entry's test; it is noted only because the entry's notes name no human work.
missing.why: One substance is not a mix, and the people were not given it to reset cell age. It does not meet or bear on the test; it is recorded so that a later reader does not count it.

records.name: A person receives cell-resetting genes in a registered trial

missing.what: The trial's registry entry (NCT07290244) gives, besides the start date and the enrolment of 18 that the entry already has, an estimated primary completion of 2027-05 and an estimated study completion of 2032-03, four sites in the United States (Boston, Charleston, Glendale and New York), status recruiting, last updated 2026-05-19, and no results posted. The entry's notes give none of these.
missing.why: The test for this entry's own rung was already met by the dose of 2026-06-09, so these dates bear only on the clinic rung. The estimate's reasoning assumes the safety study reports by 2028, and the registry's own estimated primary completion of 2027-05 is a little earlier than that, which if anything pulls the clinic rung's years forward.

missing.what: The company's release of 2026-10-08, which the entry cites, says more than the entry records: the safety board recommended going up to a second dose level of 6 times ten to the eleventh viral genomes, and in each of the two people whose visual field improved, at least 28 per cent of the field's measured points improved by more than 4 decibels.
missing.why: This entry's test asks only for a dose inside a registered trial with a public record of it, which is already met. missing.what: A longevity news site reported on 2026-10-07 that the KHL Foundation had announced that a small number of people were given an experimental eleven-gene treatment containing three of the four cell-resetting genes, outside any registered trial, one of them on 2026-03-11, through an initiative led by a named doctor. records.name: Partially resetting cells reverses ageing in a living animal

missing.what: A peer-reviewed reanalysis in the journal Aging (Meiners and colleagues, 2026-10-27) went back over the gene readings from the liver, kidney and spleen of old mice given seven months of partial resetting. In liver and kidney it found age-related inflammation turned down and age-suppressed metabolism turned back up; in the spleen it found cell division and DNA-repair programmes prominent and flagged a possible risk of lasting genetic and growth stress. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: The animal rung is already held, so this does not change the stage. It bears on the estimate's latest year, which allows for 'the safety question that hangs over the field' closing it for a generation: a peer-reviewed reading of a tissue-by-tissue risk signal is the first dated evidence in this record for that worry, which argues for keeping the late years where they are rather than pulling them in.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Neuron (Berdugo-Vega and colleagues, 2026-02-10) reports cognitive rejuvenation in mice through partial resetting of the brain cells that hold a memory. The entry does not mention it.
missing.why: On a plain reading it meets the animal rung the entry already holds ('a restored tissue function moved towards youth, compared with untreated controls, in a peer-reviewed report'), in a second organ. It makes the description out of date, which stops at 2016 and 2020, rather than moving a stage.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Aging Cell (Mallavibarrena and colleagues, 2026-11-01) reports that short bursts of the four resetting genes in ageing mice left a smaller area of brain damage after a blocked artery, with better neurological scores, preserved myelin and preserved nerve-cell density against untreated controls. The entry does not mention it; it is eight days before the date of this check, so a weekly reading may yet catch it.
missing.why: It meets the animal rung already held, by the test's words 'a restored tissue function moved towards youth, compared with untreated controls, in a peer-reviewed report'. It is the newest such report and belongs in the description rather than in a stage change.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Cell (Lu and colleagues, 2025-08-14) reports that a drift of cells towards a connective-tissue-like state, which the authors find widespread in ageing and disease, is reversed by partial resetting. The entry does not mention it.
missing.why: Listed in the literature database by title and date; its abstract was not opened here, so whether it reports a measured marker moved towards youth in a living animal against controls is unchecked. It bears on the description, which names no work after 2020.

missing.what: The company's release of 2026-10-08 gives figures the entry's description leaves out: in each of the two people whose visual field improved, at least 28 per cent of the field's measured points improved by more than 4 decibels, and the safety board recommended going up to a second dose level.
missing.why: It bears on the first-human rung, which asks for a measured marker of biological age or a restored tissue function in a person, but it does not meet it, because the settler asks for a peer-reviewed report and this is a company release of an open-label trial with no control group. If the same figures appear in a journal, the first-human rung is reached, which is earlier than the likely year of 2029.

records.name: A person's biological age, read from the marks on their DNA, falls after a treatment

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Nature Communications (Corley and colleagues, 2026-05-19) looked afterwards at the DNA marks of 84 adults in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of the weight-loss drug semaglutide (45 on the drug, 39 on placebo, 32 weeks, blood samples before and after). It reports less epigenetic ageing on several named clocks against placebo, including a pace-of-ageing clock 9 per cent slower, and the authors call the analysis exploratory and not planned in advance. The treatment's own entry does not mention it; a companion treatment on the same site does, so the fact is logged in data/.
missing.why: The test asks for a person who 'afterwards reads younger on a validated clock built from the chemical marks on their DNA, compared with before and with untreated controls, in a peer-reviewed report that names the clock and the sample'. This report names the clocks and the sample and has a placebo group, which the 2019 trial the entry rests on did not; what is unclear is whether a slower pace and a lower adjusted reading against placebo count as reading younger than before. If they do, this entry's first-human rung now rests on controlled evidence.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle (Stanfield and colleagues, 2026-04-01) gives a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of weekly rapamycin alongside exercise in 40 adults aged 65 to 85 over 13 weeks, with 'several epigenetic age measures' among its secondary outcomes. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: The abstract says clock measures were taken but does not give their result, so whether a reading fell cannot be settled from it. It bears on the estimate's reasoning that 'a controlled trial that turns a validated clock back is likely within a decade, since several are running', by naming one that has now reported.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed secondary analysis in GeroScience (Ryan and colleagues, 2026-10-29) reports on aspirin and a measure of capacity in older men and women within a randomised controlled trial. Listed in the literature database; the abstract was not opened.
missing.why: Found in a search of the literature database and not opened, so whether it reports a clock read from DNA marks is unchecked. It is recorded so that a later reading can rule it in or out.

records.name: A drug that boosts the cell's recycling of its worn parts improves an age-related function in people

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Aging Cell (Alsaleh and colleagues, 2026-06-01) gives a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled pilot trial of spermidine, 6 mg a day for 13 weeks, in 40 adults over 65 after a third covid vaccine dose. It reports that the supplement turned on the cell's recycling in immune cells and improved the antibody response, but only in those who had not responded to the vaccine, and the authors present the trial as a safety pilot. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: It does not meet the test, which asks for a pre-stated main measure of 'an age-related function (memory, heart function, muscle strength)' to improve more than placebo: this trial's stated purpose was safety, and the gain was in part of the group. It bears on the estimate towards earlier, because it is the first controlled human trial of a recycling booster since 2022 to report a benefit of any kind on the trial's own terms.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Aging and Disease (Schwarz and colleagues, 2026-10-09) gives a further analysis of brain scans from 75 people aged 60 to 90 with self-reported memory complaints in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of spermidine, 0.9 mg a day for 12 months. Blood flow in one brain region rose against placebo and one measure of white-matter structure held steady where it fell on placebo. The authors call the analysis exploratory. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: It does not meet the test: an exploratory analysis of scan measures is not the trial's pre-stated main measure, and blood flow in a brain region is not one of the functions the test names. It bears on the estimate towards earlier, because it is a mid-sized controlled trial of the kind the estimate expects to report in the early 2030s already reporting something.

missing.what: The protocol of a Danish randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (POLYCAD, Thorup and colleagues, Trials, 2025-10-30) says 187 patients aged 65 and over with coronary artery disease have been randomised to spermidine 24 mg a day or placebo for 48 weeks, with four main measures stated in advance: the mass of the heart's main pumping chamber on a scan, peak oxygen uptake, muscle mass and inflammation. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: No result yet, so the test is not met. It bears directly on the estimate, whose earliest first-human year of 2028 assumes 'a trial already running reports positive by 2029': this is that trial, fully enrolled, with heart function and muscle mass as pre-stated main measures, and a 48-week course that began before the protocol was published.

records.name: A drug breaks the sugar cross-links that stiffen old tissue

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Physiological Reports (Reeve and colleagues, 2026-06-01) gave the drug the entry is built on, alagebrium, to 20-month-old mice by mouth for four months. It did not significantly reduce stiffness in the large or brain arteries, and had no effect on blood-vessel lining function, thinking or the collagen cross-linking itself; cross-linking was higher in old than young untreated mice. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: It does not meet the animal rung, which asks for a living animal to have measurably more elastic arteries or less of the cross-link; this report is the opposite finding. It bears on the estimate towards later, and on the entry's second sentence, because the 2001 human result the record keeps as the class's first human now has a long animal study against it.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Nature Communications (Trabosh and colleagues, 2026-07-14, from the company working on this class) describes an engineered enzyme that undoes one kind of sugar damage on proteins, chosen from more than 500 million variants, and shows it undoing that damage in model proteins and in tissue samples from elderly donors. The paper says plainly that this is a proof of principle, and the damage it undoes is not the main human cross-link the entry names. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: It does not meet the animal rung, because the work is in test tubes and in tissue samples, not in a living animal. It bears on the estimate, whose reasoning says 'the current candidates had not reached animals in a peer-reviewed report' and expects an animal result by 2030: a peer-reviewed paper from the company now exists one step short of an animal.

missing.what: Two trials in the registry that the entry does not mention put the drug together with exercise: one at a university hospital in the Netherlands in 48 people, completed, last updated 2013-09-09 (NCT01417663), and one at a university medical centre in Texas in 62 people, completed, estimated primary completion 2012-06, last updated 2020-08-07 (NCT01014572). Neither has results posted.
missing.why: Whether either meets the test cannot be told from the registry, which posts no results for them; the entry's own first-human rung is already held. They bear on the description, which says the company 'ended its remaining trials in January 2009' and leaves the impression that nothing was tried after the 2011 heart-failure trial.

records.name: An antibody clears amyloid from the brain and slows the decline of Alzheimer's disease

missing.what: The European Union authorised the antibody the entry is built on, lecanemab (sold as Leqembi), on 2025-04-15, for adults with early Alzheimer's disease and confirmed amyloid in the brain who carry one copy or none of a particular risk gene. The medicines agency's own page gives that date and says the authorisation is valid throughout the Union. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: The wide-use rung asks for the drug to be 'available by prescription in several countries and taken by a substantial share of eligible patients'. With the United States, the European Union and, by other accounts, Japan and China, the first half of that is plainly met; the second half has no published figure, as the entry's own notes say. So the test is half met on the record and the entry does not show it.

missing.what: The European Union authorised the second antibody, donanemab (sold as Kisunla), on 2025-09-24, for the same narrowed group of patients. The entry says only that 'a second antibody followed in 2024', which is its United States approval.
missing.why: The clinic rung for this entry asks for a full approval for Alzheimer's disease, which it already holds. This bears on the wide-use rung in the same way as the first authorisation, by adding a second drug across the same 27 countries, and on the description, which stops at 2024 for the second antibody.

missing.what: A position paper by Alzheimer Europe dated 2026-05-04 says, by the account of a search summary, that the great majority of patients in Europe cannot get these authorised treatments through publicly funded care, and that as of September 2025 the first antibody had been launched in only Austria and Germany. Separately, by the same kind of summary, Britain's health-value body advised against both drugs in final draft guidance of 2025-06-19, both makers won appeals in January 2026, and a decision was expected later in 2026. None of this is in the entry or in data/.
missing.why: The document was fetched but came back as unreadable file data, so these facts rest on search summaries and are reported as unopened. They bear on the estimate towards later: the estimate's likely wide-use year of 2035 turns on price and on clinics able to give the drug, and the clearest dated evidence on the record now is that a European authorisation has not brought payment for it, and that Britain's value body has so far said no.

records.name: Eye drops dissolve the clouded protein of a cataract

corrections.entry_says: The description calls it 'a controlled pilot trial ... in about 40 people', and the estimate's note says '8 people enrolled by the registry's last update'.
corrections.source_says: Read on 2026-11-09, the registry entry (NCT07395986) gives an enrolment of 8 marked actual, not estimated, and a status of active and no longer recruiting, last updated 2026-08-11. On the registry's own record the trial has stopped taking part and will not reach about 40 people.

corrections.entry_says: The estimate's note calls the trial 'randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled'.
corrections.source_says: The registry's masking field gives four masked parties: the participant, the care provider, the investigator and the person assessing the outcome. The trial's own official title does say 'Double-Masked', so the entry follows the title rather than the field.

missing.what: The registry entry also gives 21 sites across the United States and an estimated primary completion of 2027-02, which the entry has. The change since the entry was written is the status, now active and no longer recruiting, with 8 people enrolled as an actual figure.
missing.why: The first-human rung asks for drops to give measurably clearer lenses in a person in a controlled trial, which a trial with 8 people and no published result does not meet. It bears on the estimate, whose clinic years were brought in on this trial's dates and its path to a late-stage trial: a pilot that closed at 8 of about 40 people is a weaker base for that path than the note assumes.

missing.what: A peer-reviewed report in Nature Communications (Song and colleagues, 2025-09-26) raised the amount of the same natural molecule inside the lens of rats by delivering, into the eye, the instructions for the enzyme that makes it, and reports a marked improvement of cataract in two rat models. It is not drops of the molecule itself, and the delivery was by injection into the eye rather than a drop. The entry does not mention it, and nothing in data/ does.
missing.why: It does not meet the animal rung as written, which asks for 'a living animal with cataracts given eye drops' and for a second group to have repeated it. It bears on the entry's replication question all the same, because it is the first peer-reviewed report since 2015 in which raising this molecule in a living animal's lens improved a cataract, by a different group and a different route.

missing.what: Two trade reports of 2026-07-15 and 2026-07-16 cover the first patient in the pilot trial, and one says the first patient was enrolled at a site in California. They are further accounts of the release the entry already cites. Seen in search summaries only.
missing.why: Nothing in them is new beyond the company's release of 2026-07-14, and they were not opened. They are recorded so that a later reading does not take them for fresh news.
